name: Linux SCTP root
tile_line: Needs code on the box. No stable kernel fix yet.
tldr: A Linux kernel SCTP bug lets any local user, even one inside a container, take over the machine. It was shown working, and no stable kernel has the fix yet. If untrusted code runs on your servers and you don't use SCTP, block the sctp module.
summary: Xint chained it with [nginx2root](/nginx2root/) to get root on the host and escape a Docker container. The fix reached the main kernel tree on 19 Nov; the only distro kernels we found with it are Gentoo's and Fedora Rawhide's, Fedora's development branch. The bug makes the kernel free memory twice or use it after freeing it.

affected.label: Kernel 4.15+ or a backport
affected.text: Xint dates the bug to 4.15 (Jan 2018). The fix names the change that caused it, and that change was also copied into older stable kernels in early 2018: 4.14.16, 4.9.79, 4.4.114, 4.1.50, 3.18.93, 3.16.55 and 3.2.100. So an older version number doesn't rule you out. The fix was merged into the main kernel tree on 19 Nov and first came out in 7.4-rc4 (22 Nov), a test release. The newest stable kernels (7.3.6, 6.18.65, 6.12.119, released 23 Nov) don't have it, and on 28 Nov it wasn't in any of the stable queues (7.3, 6.18, 6.12, 6.6, 6.1, 5.15, 5.10); the only distro kernels we found carrying it are Gentoo's kernel sources and Fedora Rawhide's 7.4-rc4 snapshot builds (Rawhide is Fedora's development branch, not a release). Xint hasn't named the fix, but the commit credits Xint's tool and matches its description.

affected.label: Untrusted code can run on it
affected.text: The attacker must already run code on the machine, as any user or inside a container. Xint got there through nginx2root. The bug needs no special rights. Containers don't stop it: they share the host kernel, Docker's default seccomp profile doesn't block SCTP sockets, and Kubernetes pods run without seccomp unless you turn it on.

affected.label: SCTP can load
affected.text: The kernel loads the sctp module the first time any program opens an SCTP socket, unless it's blocked. Many distros ship it. Red Hat says it isn't loaded by default on RHEL: it's in kernel-modules-extra, which blacklists it on install. If `lsmod` prints nothing, it can still load on demand; `modprobe -c | grep sctp` shows any block.

do.label: Block SCTP if you don't use it
do.text: Put this line in a file under /etc/modprobe.d/ (Ubuntu uses disable-sctp.conf); on Debian and Ubuntu, then run `sudo update-initramfs -u`. It doesn't unload a module that's already loaded (reboot, or `sudo rmmod sctp` if nothing uses it) and doesn't help if SCTP is built into the kernel. It breaks telecom signalling and some Kubernetes network plugins. Red Hat's version is `install sctp /bin/true` plus `blacklist sctp`.

do.label: Update the kernel and reboot
do.text: Install your distro's kernel with the fix ("sctp: do not free a new asoc peeled off while sendmsg slept") once it ships, then reboot. The 23 Nov stable releases (7.3.6, 6.18.65, 6.12.119) don't have it, and on 28 Nov it wasn't in any of the stable queues (7.3, 6.18, 6.12, 6.6, 6.1, 5.15, 5.10); Debian unstable's 7.3.6-1 doesn't have it either. No release date is announced and the fix has no CVE yet; we'll check again by 2 Dec 2026.

do.label: Patch the way in
do.text: Xint's chain starts with nginx2root, so upgrade nginx too. Any other way to run code on the host or in a container works just as well.
